status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: High pole is consistently 'more punitive / more police power'.

items.stem: Should spending on police in most US cities go up or down?
items.scope: Think about cities in general, not only your own.
options: Replace police departments with other public-safety services
Cut it a lot and move the money to social services
Cut it somewhat and move some money to social services
Keep it about the same
Increase it somewhat, to hire and train more officers
Increase it a lot, to hire and train many more officers

items.stem: Who should respond to 911 calls about someone having a mental health crisis?
items.scope: Calls where no weapon or violence has been reported.
options: Trained mental health workers, without police
Mental health workers together with police
Police officers with mental health training

items.stem: Should people be able to sue individual police officers who violate their constitutional rights?
items.scope: Lawsuits for money damages, not criminal charges.
items.context: A legal rule called qualified immunity blocks most such suits unless an earlier court case found nearly identical conduct illegal.
options: Yes; end qualified immunity
Narrow it, so officers can be sued for serious violations even without an identical earlier case
Keep it as it is
Expand legal protections for officers

definitions.text: A court-made rule that protects government officials from personal lawsuits unless they violated a clearly established right.
definitions.source: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982); Pearson v. Callahan (2009)

items.stem: Should records of complaints about police misconduct be public?
items.scope: Complaints about things like excessive force or dishonesty.
options: Yes, all complaints, including ones not proven
Only complaints found to be true
No; keep them confidential

items.stem: Should judges be required to give minimum prison sentences for certain crimes, such as drug dealing?
items.scope: Minimum sentences set by law that judges cannot go below.
options: No; end mandatory minimums and let judges decide
Keep them only for violent crimes
Keep them as they are
Add more of them and make them longer

items.stem: For violent crimes such as armed robbery and serious assault, how long are US prison sentences?
items.scope: Think about typical sentences, not one case.
options: Much too long
Somewhat too long
About right
Somewhat too short
Much too short

items.stem: Should the death penalty be used for murder?
items.scope: Cases where guilt is not in doubt. Other crimes come next.
options: Never
Only for the most extreme murders, such as killing several people or a child
For most planned murders

items.stem: Should the death penalty also be possible for each of these crimes?
items.scope: Answer each case separately. Guilt is not in doubt.
options: Should not be possible
Should be possible

cases.text: A terrorist attack that kills people
Running a large drug trafficking operation

items.stem: Before trial, how should it be decided who stays in jail?
items.scope: People charged with a crime but not yet convicted.
options: End cash bail; release almost everyone except those who are a clear danger
Release most people charged with nonviolent crimes without bail; judges set bail for others
Keep cash bail, with amounts set by judges
Keep everyone charged with violent or repeat crimes in jail until trial

items.stem: Which should prisons focus on more?

sides.label: Rehabilitation
sides.text: Education and treatment to prepare people for release, even if it costs more.

sides.label: Punishment
sides.text: Punishing crime and protecting the public, even if fewer people change their ways.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: After people finish their sentences, which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Think of people convicted of nonviolent crimes.

sides.label: Second chances
sides.text: Limit how employers and landlords can use criminal records, even if they take on some risk.

sides.label: Free to consider records
sides.text: Let employers and landlords freely consider records, even if it's harder for people to rebuild their lives.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.stem: Should teenagers aged 15 to 17 accused of serious violent crimes be tried as adults?
items.scope: Crimes like armed robbery or killing someone.
options: Never; always in juvenile court
Only for murder
For serious violent crimes, if a judge decides
Yes, automatically for serious violent crimes

items.stem: Should governments use private companies to run prisons and immigration detention centers?
items.scope: Companies paid by government to hold people.
options: No; ban them
Only under strict oversight
Yes, if they save money

items.stem: What should happen to protesters who block a highway or major road?
options: Allow it if it's brief and peaceful
Ask them to move, and arrest only those who refuse
Arrest them right away
Arrest them and treat it as a serious crime, with possible jail time

items.stem: When a protest turns into rioting and looting, what should authorities do?
options: Use as little force as possible and focus on calming tensions
Arrest people damaging property, but avoid force against peaceful protesters
Use whatever force is needed to stop it quickly, including the National Guard

items.stem: Should the president be able to send troops into a US city to fight crime, over the state governor's objection?
items.scope: National Guard or active-duty troops. Answer for any president of either party.
options: Never over a governor's objection
Only during a riot or uprising local police can't control
Yes, whenever the president judges crime is out of control

items.stem: How much weight should crime victims' views carry when judges decide sentences and parole boards decide on release?
items.scope: Victims or their families speaking about the offender.
options: None; decisions should rest on the law and the offender
Victims can speak, but their wishes get no special weight
Victims' views should carry significant weight

items.stem: Should police be able to take cash or property they suspect is linked to a crime, without convicting the owner?
items.scope: Called civil asset forfeiture. The owner can go to court to get it back.
options: No; only after a criminal conviction
Only with strong evidence, and the government must prove its case
Yes, as most states allow today
items.notes: Expected to cross-cut: libertarian and left opposition.

items.stem: Should police be able to stop and pat down people they find suspicious in high-crime areas?
items.scope: Stops without an arrest, based on an officer's suspicion.
options: No
Only with specific reasons, recorded and reviewed for bias
Yes, it helps prevent crime
